title: Ang 14: Sri Rag begins
hookLine: the first raga opens with Guru Nanak's palaces of pearls
tomorrow: what do sweet, salty and sour have to do with God?

lines: A HOUSE TOUR ON YOUR FEED.
cards: Scroll long enough and someone is giving a tour of a house with a pool that runs off the edge of a cliff. Marble, glass, a closet the size of a bedroom. It's hard not to want it a little.
Ang fourteen opens the Granth's raga order with a house like that, built of pearls. And then the hymn asks what owning it might cost.

teach.h: SRI RAG, MAHALA 1: THE FIRST RAGA.
teach.b: The heading reads Sri Rag, Mahala 1: Guru Nanak, in the first raga of the order.

In paraphrase: if I had a palace built of pearls, set with jewels, scented with musk and saffron, sandalwood and aloe, let it not be that, seeing it, I forget You, and Your Name no longer comes to mind. Then the ifs grow.
A floor of diamonds and rubies. The powers of a siddha, a yogi who can vanish at will. A sultan's throne and an army.
Each time, the same plea: let me not forget You. Readers take this two ways. The first: the hymn piles up riches to show how easily they pull a heart away.
A simpler life leaves less to forget behind. The second: the hymn's fear is forgetting, not owning.
Sikh teaching asks householders to earn honestly, kirat karni, and to share, vand chhakna, and this same hymn sets a yogi's powers and a throne beside the pearls.

teach.h: ONE: RICHES PULL THE HEART AWAY.

teach.b: Something to tell someone tonight: the Granth's raga order opens with neither a praise of wealth nor a rule against it, but with a plea: let me not forget.
Both readings keep that plea at the center.

how: The Guru Granth Sahib's raga sections begin with Sri Rag on ang 14; Sikhs read and sing its hymns in the gurdwara and at home, and Sikh teaching pairs honest work (kirat karni) with sharing (vand chhakna).

o: the page that closes the Sohila, the night prayer

games.q: the palace hymn — tap the pairs.
p: the first raga of the order

s: Sri Rag is the first raga in the Granth's raga order
it begins on ang 14, under the heading Sri Rag, Mahala 1.
the palace hymn says owning a palace is a sin
its plea is: let it not be that, seeing it, I forget You.
the hymn only talks about money
it also imagines a yogi's powers and a sultan's throne.

games.q: your uncle says the palace hymn means a Sikh family shouldn't buy a big house. you read it differently. what's his strongest case?
o: the hymn piles up riches to show how easily they pull a heart away.
the Gurus taught that money itself is unclean and must be avoided.
the Sikh code sets a limit on the size of a family's home.
games.why: that's his view at its best. yours: the hymn's fear is forgetting, not owning, and it sets a yogi's powers and a throne beside the pearls.

practice: If you have the page, read the hymn's first line on ang fourteen. Then count three good things you have right now, a room, a person, a meal, one on each slow breath. After each, pause for a moment and remember where it came from.

wordCard.voice: Ang 14. Where Sri Rag begins, the first raga, with Guru Nanak's palace of pearls and its plea not to forget. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Sirirag, Sri Rag, the first raga of the Granth's raga order, as spelled in the heading on ang 14.

carryVoice: Keep this: the first raga opens with a palace and a single plea, let me not forget. Take care.
